opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the deepest questions about what true creativity really is. If you look at where AI systems are today, they're getting incredibly good at solving well-specified problems. You give them a clear objective, a math problem with a known answer, a game like Go with a defined win condition, or a protein structure to predict, and they can search through enormous spaces of possibilities and find remarkable solutions. AlphaGo's Move 37 was a good example of that: genuinely creative, something no human had played, but still within the confines of the game.

Coming up with a great conjecture is a different kind of thing. It's not finding the answer to a question; it's figuring out which question is worth asking in the first place. Think about the Riemann hypothesis, or what Einstein did with relativity. That requires taste, judgment, a sense of what's interesting, what's fruitful, what's going to open up whole new fields. There's no clear objective function for that. How do you score whether a conjecture is "good" before you even know if it's true, or before anyone has seen what it leads to decades later?

I sometimes describe it as levels of creativity. There's interpolation, averaging what you've seen. There's extrapolation, like Move 37, going beyond the data but within a framework. And then there's invention, actually coming up with the game itself, the new framework. Inventing Go, not just playing a brilliant move in it. That top level is what the great scientists do, and I don't think our systems are there yet.

It's also about building really deep models of the world, having an intuitive sense of where the gaps in our understanding are and where the beautiful, elegant explanations might be hiding. That's what I'd consider one of the real hallmarks of AGI. If a system could come up with something like general relativity given only the information Einstein had back then, that would be a pretty convincing test. So for me, it's one of the most exciting things we're working towards, but it's also one of the hardest, precisely because it's so hard even to define what success looks like.

r001.rationale: It says originating a conjecture means deciding which question is worth asking and requires judgment about what is interesting and fruitful.

r002.rationale: It mentions Einstein’s relativity as an example of a scientific leap, but does not say that the mechanism behind such leaps remains unclear.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it comes down to what the search space looks like in each case. When you're solving a conjecture, you've been handed the target. Someone has already done the hard work of saying, here is a precise statement, and it's probably true, and it probably matters. The system then has an extremely well-defined objective, and if it's mathematics, you even get a verifier for free in something like Lean. So you can search, you can get a signal, and that's exactly the kind of regime where these systems, the AlphaGo lineage if you like, have been incredibly strong. Vast search space, but a clear objective and a clear reward.

Coming up with the conjecture in the first place is a different kind of problem altogether. There's no reward function sitting there. The space of true statements is essentially infinite, and almost all of them are completely uninteresting. The hard part isn't generating true things, it's picking out the one that's deep, that unifies two areas nobody thought were connected, that opens up a whole new direction. That's taste, really. It's judgment about what matters, and that's something the great mathematicians and scientists have in a way that's quite hard to articulate even for them. Ramanujan is the classic example, writing down these extraordinary identities without proofs, and it took a century to understand why some of them were so important.

So the second problem is about asking the right question rather than answering it, and I've always felt that's the deeper form of intelligence. In some ways it's what I'd want to see before I'd say a system was genuinely creative in the scientific sense. We're making progress on the first. I think the second is still some way off, and it's one of the things I'd most like to see us crack.

r001.rationale: It says the hard part is selecting a conjecture that is deep, significant, and opens a new direction, distinguishing that from merely generating true statements.

r002.rationale: It describes scientific judgment as hard to articulate, but does not state that the mechanism behind imaginative leaps such as Einstein’s development of relativity remains unclear.

astra-6.text:
Well, when you’re trying to solve a conjecture, somebody has already framed the question for you. You have a target, and in mathematics you have a very precise way of checking whether you’ve reached it: does the proof hold up?

Coming up with the conjecture is much more open-ended. What should you ask in the first place? There are infinitely many statements you could make, but most of them are uninteresting. You want something that’s true, surprising, and that reveals some deeper structure—perhaps connecting things that previously seemed unrelated.

So that requires more than being able to search for a solution. It requires a kind of taste: an understanding of what matters and what might open up a whole new area of inquiry. And that’s much harder to specify as an objective. How do you tell a system, ‘Find me a question that’s worth spending the next ten years answering’?

I don’t think that’s beyond AI in principle. But I think choosing the right question is a deeper test of scientific creativity than answering a question we’ve already identified as important.

r001.rationale: It says most possible conjectures are uninteresting and that identifying a question worth pursuing requires taste and understanding what matters.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Einstein, relativity, or that the mechanism behind such imaginative leaps remains unclear.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, solving a conjecture, however difficult it is, gives you a target. Somebody has already framed the question, and you have some way of knowing whether you’ve answered it. Coming up with the conjecture means deciding what the right question is in the first place.

And the word “important” is doing a lot of work there. You could generate endless conjectures that are true but trivial, or questions that are difficult but don’t lead anywhere. The challenge is to identify something that’s both tractable and profound—something that, if you resolved it, would reveal a deeper structure or open up a whole new area of science.

That requires a kind of taste and judgment about the space of possible ideas. You have to understand what’s missing from our current understanding, and imagine what might connect those gaps. I think AI will eventually be able to do that, but it’s a much more open-ended challenge than finding a solution to a question we’ve already specified.

r001.rationale: It says important conjectures must be distinguished from true but trivial or unproductive ones, requiring judgment about which ideas are profound and worth pursuing.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss Einstein, relativity, or the uncertainty about how imaginative scientific leaps happen.
